book_title: CM2013 — Signal Processing and Data Analytics in Biomedical Engineering
book_subtitle: Demo notebooks, labs, and capstone tracks

notebooks.title: Biosignals & Medical Images
notebooks.question: Where do the wiggles in an ECG or EEG actually come from, and what makes a signal 'hard'?
concepts: Origins of ECG / EEG / EMG and their signatures (EOG: amplitude/bandwidth only)
Amplitude, bandwidth and rhythm as a signal 'fingerprint'
Deterministic vs stochastic; stationary vs non-stationary
notebooks.task: You'll generate synthetic ECG, EEG, and EMG signals, compare their amplitude/bandwidth/rhythm "fingerprints," and practice identifying each from its signature alone — predicting the change before you run each cell.

notebooks.title: Lab 01 — The biosignal zoo & an acquisition audit
notebooks.question: Is this recording fit for the question I want to ask of it?
concepts: Chapter 1 — §1.4 (biosignal signatures), §1.6 (the taxonomy), §1.8 (task types), §1.9 (the pipeline).
notebooks.task: You'll load a synthetic ECG, name what's visible in the raw trace, then build a one-page acquisition-audit checklist (clipping, flatline, bandwidth-vs-task detectors) and prove it fires only on defective recordings — the first thing to run on any new signal.

notebooks.title: Sampling, Aliasing & Quantization
notebooks.question: How does a continuous voltage become discrete numbers without lying about the truth?
concepts: Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem and the Nyquist frequency
Aliasing and why it is irreversible
Quantization SNR ≈ 6.02·N + 1.76 dB and crest-factor headroom
Anti-alias filtering and the guard band
Spatial / imaging sampling: moiré and Radon (CT) undersampling
notebooks.task: You'll sample a tone below and above the Nyquist rate to watch aliasing appear (and see why it can't be undone), check quantization SNR against the 6.02·N + 1.76 dB rule, and explore spatial undersampling (moiré, CT streaks).

notebooks.title: Lab 02 — Sampling, aliasing & clock drift
notebooks.question: Is my sampling rate and timing good enough for the question I am asking?
concepts: Chapter 2 — §2.7–§2.9 (Nyquist, aliasing, quantization), §2.13 (non-uniform sampling & resampling).
notebooks.task: You'll predict then confirm an aliased 40 Hz tone's fold-down frequency, show that more ADC bits never fix an alias, and track how a 0.1% clock-rate mismatch between two channels produces a timing drift no fixed resample can remove.

notebooks.title: Fourier Analysis, FFT & Time–Frequency
notebooks.question: How do we see the delta, theta, alpha and spindle 'notes' hidden inside a raw EEG trace?
concepts: Fourier series, the Gibbs phenomenon, and the FFT's O(N log N) win
Frequency resolution Δf = fs/N vs zero-padding (interpolation ≠ resolution)
The STFT and the spectrogram; the uncertainty trade-off
2-D FFT of an image: magnitude vs phase, and the inverse FFT
One operation, two domains: convolve↔multiply, smooth↔low-pass
notebooks.task: You'll rebuild a square wave from harmonics to see the Gibbs phenomenon, compare zero-padding against a genuinely longer record to see which one actually improves resolution, build a spectrogram, and reconstruct an image from FFT magnitude vs. phase alone.

notebooks.title: Lab 03 — Representation: the STFT vs the global spectrum
notebooks.question: Is one global spectrum enough, or does the signal's content change over time — and *when*?
concepts: Chapter 3 — §3.9–§3.10 (STFT/spectrogram and the uncertainty trade-off), §3.7 (resolution vs zero-padding).
notebooks.task: You'll compute a signal's global spectrum, then its spectrogram, then sweep the STFT window length to measure — not just claim — the time/frequency uncertainty trade-off, confirming a real alpha-to-spindle frequency shift only a windowed view can reveal.

notebooks.title: Windowing & Spectral Leakage
notebooks.question: Why does a clean sinusoid smear across neighbouring frequencies, and which window fixes it?
concepts: The finite-length problem and the origin of spectral leakage
Window functions (rect, Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Kaiser, Tukey)
Main-lobe width, side-lobe level, ENBW, scalloping loss
The resolution–leakage trade-off, quantified
Choosing a window for ECG / EEG / EMG
notebooks.task: You'll compare five window functions on the same two-tone signal, measure their main-lobe/side-lobe trade-off directly, and sweep a Kaiser window's β to watch resolution and leakage move in opposite directions.

notebooks.title: Lab 04 — Windowing & the leakage↔resolution trade
notebooks.question: Which window lets me see the peaks I care about — without leakage burying a weak one?
concepts: Chapter 4 — §4.2–§4.5 (leakage, window functions, window properties, the resolution↔leakage trade), §4.6 (selection guidelines).
notebooks.task: You'll test whether five windows can resolve two close equal-amplitude tones, then whether they can reveal a tone 60 dB weaker than its neighbour, and show numerically that the window that wins one task always loses the other.

notebooks.title: Wavelets & Other Transforms
notebooks.question: When a single spectrum is not enough — how do we localize a transient K-complex in time and frequency?
concepts: Multiresolution time–frequency tiling (tall-thin vs short-wide)
DWT levels mapped to EEG bands; the Hilbert envelope for EMG
2-D DWT subband pyramid (LL/LH/HL/HH) on an image
Inverse transform & perfect reconstruction
Wavelet compression & denoising
notebooks.task: You'll localize a K-complex with the DWT and check which decomposition level it lands on, pull an EMG envelope out with the Hilbert transform, and run wavelet compression and denoising on a 2-D image via its subbands.

notebooks.title: Lab 05 — Choosing a transform: CWT / DWT / Hilbert
notebooks.question: Which representation fits THIS signal's time–frequency structure — and does each part get the *right notion of 'frequency'*?
concepts: Chapter 5 — §5.3–§5.5 (CWT/DWT, localizing a K-complex, the Hilbert envelope).
notebooks.task: You'll localise a transient's exact instant with a CWT, find which DWT detail level carries it, and recover an AM burst's amplitude envelope with the Hilbert transform — then check each transform actually answered the question it was built for.

notebooks.title: Stochastic Processes & AR/ARMA Modelling
notebooks.question: Biosignals are partly random — how do we describe and model that randomness usefully?
concepts: Stationarity: strict, wide-sense, and local/quasi-stationary
Autocorrelation, PACF, and the Wiener–Khinchin theorem
AR / MA / ARMA models as compact signal descriptions
Order selection with AIC / MDL
Why a global spectrum hides 30-second stage changes
notebooks.task: You'll compare the autocorrelation of a periodic signal against noise, read an AR model's order straight off an ACF/PACF pair, then sweep the AR order on an EEG spectrum and watch it go from under- to over-fit.

notebooks.title: Lab 06 — AR modelling: fit, order, and residual checks
notebooks.question: Does my AR model actually fit — or is it hallucinating a peak?
concepts: Chapter 6 — §6.6–§6.8 (AR/MA/ARMA, order selection via ACF/PACF, an AR spectrum with a real peak), §6.3 (autocorrelation).
notebooks.task: You'll fit AR models by hand via Yule-Walker at growing orders to see under- and over-fitting, pick the order objectively with an information criterion, and use residual whiteness — not a pretty spectrum — to decide whether the fit is trustworthy.

notebooks.title: Spectral Estimation
notebooks.question: The raw periodogram is noisy and unreliable — how do we get a spectrum we can trust?
concepts: Why the periodogram is inconsistent (variance does not fall with N)
Bartlett & Welch: averaging to cut variance (≈1/K)
Multitaper (Slepian/DPSS) estimation
Parametric AR spectra via Yule–Walker / Burg
HRV band power (LF/HF) as a worked example
notebooks.task: You'll watch a periodogram's variance fail to shrink as the record gets longer, then compare Welch, multitaper, and parametric AR estimates on the same epoch, finishing with an HRV LF/HF band-power worked example.

notebooks.title: Lab 07 — Spectral estimator choice & the robust-peak checklist
notebooks.question: Is this spectral peak real — and which estimator should I trust?
concepts: Chapter 7 — §7.2 (why the periodogram is inconsistent), §7.5 (Welch's method), §7.9 (model-order selection and the decision framework).
notebooks.task: You'll watch the periodogram's variance refuse to shrink with more data while Welch's does, then run a robust-peak checklist on a real 10 Hz rhythm and a fake periodogram bump to see it correctly pass one and fail the other.

notebooks.title: Noise & Artifacts
notebooks.question: Before removing noise, can we name it? Powerline hum, baseline sway, muscle bursts, blinks.
concepts: Noise colours: white, pink (1/f), brown; PSD slope
Powerline interference and its harmonics
Impulsive / salt-and-pepper noise; baseline wander & motion
Quality control BEFORE preprocessing
Diagnose the noise before choosing the tool
notebooks.task: You'll build a noise "line-up" (white/pink/brown) and classify each by its PSD slope, then identify powerline interference and impulsive/salt-and-pepper artifacts by their signatures before picking a fix.

notebooks.title: Lab 08 — A QC screen and the 'what must survive' question
notebooks.question: Is this recording fit — and what must a correction NOT damage?
concepts: Chapter 8 — §8.2 (quality control before preprocessing), §8.6 (powerline interference), §8.8 (baseline wander), §8.11 (the diagnostic decision framework).
notebooks.task: You'll build detectors for mains hum, baseline wander, and motion bursts, classify each as remove/mark/source/failed before touching a filter, then prove a proper notch preserves the ECG's ST level while a naive high-pass destroys it.

notebooks.title: Digital Filter Design (1-D & 2-D)
notebooks.question: How do we keep the spindles and drop the hum — and why is despiking an image the same trick as despiking an ECG?
concepts: LTI systems and convolution (the impulse response slid along)
IIR (Butterworth) design as second-order sections for stability
Zero-phase filtfilt vs a real-time causal filter
Linear vs non-linear: median/Savitzky-Golay beat the mean on outliers
2-D spatial filtering and the Pan–Tompkins QRS detector
notebooks.task: You'll compare zero-phase filtfilt against a real-time causal filter, watch a median filter beat a mean filter on outlier removal, and run the Pan–Tompkins QRS detector end to end on a synthetic ECG.

notebooks.title: Lab 09 — Filter an EEG — and prove delta survived
notebooks.question: Can I remove drift, muscle, and mains from sleep EEG without damaging the delta rhythm that defines deep sleep?
concepts: Chapter 9 — §9.4–§9.6 (FIR vs IIR, zero-phase filtering and edge transients, the EEG band-pass + 50 Hz notch).
notebooks.task: You'll design a band-pass-plus-notch EEG filter, measure how filtfilt's two-pass response squares the one-pass attenuation at the cutoff, and confirm delta band-power survives filtering — then watch a naive 2 Hz high-pass destroy it instead.

notebooks.title: Noise Reduction & Signal Enhancement
notebooks.question: When a filter can't separate signal from noise because they overlap in frequency, what else works?
concepts: Ensemble averaging and the √N SNR law
Adaptive filtering (LMS) with a reference channel
Wavelet-threshold denoising
ICA / PCA for artifact removal
Matching the enhancement to the noise type
notebooks.task: You'll verify the √N ensemble-averaging law directly, cancel a correlated artifact with an LMS adaptive filter, and compare wavelet-threshold denoising against ICA/PCA for pulling out unwanted components.

notebooks.title: Lab 10 — Enhancement failure modes: did I recover the signal or manufacture one?
notebooks.question: Did my enhancement recover the *true* signal, or manufacture a plausible-looking one?
concepts: Chapter 10 — §10.3 (the √N law and its assumptions), §10.5 (LMS adaptive filtering), §10.7 (ICA/PCA unmixing), §10.8 (method-selection guidelines).
notebooks.task: You'll confirm the √N averaging law empirically across N=1 to 64, use an LMS adaptive filter to cancel a motion artifact correlated with a reference channel, and unmix two ICA sources — checking each time whether the signal was recovered or merely manufactured.

notebooks.title: Feature Engineering & Selection
notebooks.question: A classifier can't read a waveform — what numbers summarise a 30-s epoch well enough to name its sleep stage?
concepts: Time and frequency features from an epoch (RMS, Hjorth, band power)
Spectral entropy; the feature-scaling leakage trap
Ranking features by mutual information; a 2-D LDA projection
ECG fiducial-point features; early vs late multi-channel fusion
notebooks.task: You'll compute time- and frequency-domain features (RMS, Hjorth parameters, band power, spectral entropy) from an epoch, rank them by mutual information, and see directly how fitting a scaler on the wrong data leaks information.

notebooks.title: Lab 11 — Features & selection with leakage controls
notebooks.question: Which features separate the sleep stages — and does my feature / selection / scaling pipeline secretly *leak*?
concepts: Chapter 11 — §11.3–§11.4 (feature families; features that separate sleep stages), §11.6–§11.7 (scaling and the leakage it hides; selection).
notebooks.task: You'll rank features by mutual information on training data only, then deliberately leak by fitting a scaler and selector on the whole dataset with a random split, and measure the exact accuracy gap against the honest, subject-grouped alternative.

notebooks.title: Lab — The design clinic — several good answers, and some wrong ones
notebooks.question: Which feature design should a wearable sleep stager use — and can you *defend* it against a reasonable alternative *and* recognise the choices that would be simply wrong?
concepts: Chapter 11 — §11.3–§11.4 (feature families; features that separate sleep stages), §11.7 (selection and the curse of dimensionality) — drawing on Chapter 4 §4.4–§4.5 (window main-lobe width and the resolution↔leakage trade) and Chapter 7 §7.5 (Welch: resolution traded against variance). A **synthesis exercise, positioned after Chapter 11**, not tied to any single chapter's lecture.
notebooks.task: You'll compare two feature-stage designs against a wearable sleep-stager spec, use the real segment-length trade-off to justify a Welch setting, and identify two feature designs that are simply wrong for the spec — not imperfect — because they can't see what the classes need distinguished.

notebooks.title: The ML Pipeline: Validation & Leakage
notebooks.question: How do we know a 90%-accurate sleep scorer isn't fooling us — and will it work on a patient it has never seen?
concepts: Train/val/test, bias–variance, and overfitting
Subject-independent validation: LOSO / GroupKFold
The six canonical data-leakage failures and their fixes
Class imbalance; kappa, macro-F1, balanced accuracy
Calibration, abstention, and 'labels are measurements too'
notebooks.task: You'll compare a naive random split against subject-independent LOSO validation on the same data to see the leakage gap directly, then work through the ROC/PR trade-off and calibration under class imbalance.

notebooks.title: Lab 12 — Imbalance & the accuracy illusion — the metric that cannot be fooled
notebooks.question: My sleep scorer is 79% accurate. Is it any good — and would I notice if it had never once detected N1?
concepts: Chapter 12 — §12.5 (class imbalance and honest metrics), §12.4 (the failure-case clinic, Failure 5).
notebooks.task: You'll read a class-imbalanced cohort's prevalence, score a real classifier on a four-metric panel (accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro-F1, kappa), then shift the decision rule by dividing by class priors and watch the model ranking flip depending on which metric you trust.

notebooks.title: Classical Learning & Unsupervised Analysis
notebooks.question: Given a clean feature matrix, which learner should score the sleep — and can structure be found without labels?
concepts: k-NN, SVM (kernel trick), decision trees, random forests
Bagging and out-of-bag error
k-means and hierarchical clustering
PCA vs feature selection
The 'fair fight': same split, same features, same metrics
notebooks.task: You'll train k-NN, an SVM, and a random forest on the identical split and features — the "fair fight" — and compare their decision boundaries, then run k-means, hierarchical clustering, and PCA on the same data.

notebooks.title: Lab 13 — A fair learner comparison — which classifier really wins on a new subject?
notebooks.question: Which classifier is really best for new subjects — and did I compare them fairly?
concepts: Chapter 13 — §13.3–§13.4 (four ways to draw a fence; three learners on the same folds).
notebooks.task: You'll fit a random forest and score it on its own training rows to see a worthless ~1.00, then compare k-NN, SVM, and a forest fairly on identical subject-independent folds against a majority-class floor to find which model really wins on a new subject.

notebooks.title: Deep Learning & Foundation Models
notebooks.question: What if the model learned its own features — and had already 'read' millions of hours of signals first?
concepts: Neurons, layers, loss, backpropagation
The CNN convolution IS Chapter 9's convolution, learned
Sequence models and attention across epochs
Self-supervised pretraining & time-series foundation models
Transfer learning and a fair comparison with the forest
notebooks.task: You'll see a CNN's convolution laid directly against Chapter 9's classical convolution, train a tiny CNN on spectrogram images, and run a fair, same-split comparison against the Chapter 13 random forest.

notebooks.title: Lab 14 — A learned model on spectrograms vs a well-featured forest — fairly
notebooks.question: Does a model that *learns* from the raw time–frequency image beat a hand-featured forest here — and is the comparison **fair**?
concepts: Chapter 14 — §14.4 (CNNs), §14.7 (practical reality: a fair fight with the forest).
notebooks.task: You'll train an MLP directly on raw spectrogram pixels against a random forest on 12 hand-chosen band-power features, score both on identical folds, then sweep training-subject count to see whether the learned model's gap is a real ceiling or just data-starvation.

notebooks.title: Deployment: Edge, Embedded & Cloud
notebooks.question: A sleep scorer in a notebook helps nobody — how does it become a wristband, a service, or a cloud API?
concepts: The edge → embedded → server → cloud spectrum
What leaves the device: raw signal vs features vs decision
Quantization and pruning: measured size/latency trade-offs
MLOps, privacy, and regulatory pathways (discussed in the book text; not modelled in this notebook)
notebooks.task: You'll measure the actual size and latency trade-off from quantizing and pruning a model, and work through what data leaves the device at each point on the edge-to-cloud spectrum.

notebooks.title: Capstone: Automatic Sleep Scoring
notebooks.question: How do all the earlier threads become one working, defensible system?
concepts: The end-to-end pipeline as reusable modules
Iterative build: baseline → tuned ensemble
Subject-independent (LOSO) evaluation, kappa & macro-F1
Confusion matrix, hypnogram, and clinical summaries
Reproducibility, and honest reporting of illustrative numbers
notebooks.task: You'll assemble the sleep-scoring pipeline's modules end to end, run an iterative baseline-to-tuned-ensemble build, and evaluate it with subject-independent LOSO kappa, a confusion matrix, and a hypnogram.

notebooks.title: Lab 16 — Capstone scaffold — build, validate, defend
notebooks.question: Can I deliver an honest end-to-end sleep-staging system and defend every design choice?
concepts: Chapter 16 — §16.2 (the pipeline as reusable modules), §16.4 (design decisions and their justification), §16.5 (evaluation in practice).
notebooks.task: You'll fill in a design-justification matrix and a what-must-survive audit for your own capstone pipeline (resampling, filter, features, split, metric) as a planning worksheet — no code here; you build the real pipeline afterward in ch16_capstone.ipynb.

notebooks.title: Real-data track — Human activity (UCI-HAR, IMU)
notebooks.question: Can self-built features tell static from walking from stairs, and why subject-wise split?
concepts: UCI-HAR raw inertial end-to-end (the gentle on-ramp)
Windowing + per-axis + dominant-frequency features
Split by subject; GroupKFold; walk↔stairs confusion
notebooks.task: You'll run the full UCI-HAR pipeline on real raw accelerometer data — window it, extract per-axis features, classify six activities with a subject-aware split, and see exactly where walk and stairs get confused.

notebooks.title: Real-data track — Sleep staging (Sleep-EDF)
notebooks.question: Does the pipeline hold up on real overnight EEG with messy labels and a subject split?
concepts: Sleep-EDF Expanded end-to-end (PhysioNet, ODC-BY)
R&K → AASM labels; split by subject, not night
Honest panel (κ, macro-F1, confusion) under LOSO + hypnogram
notebooks.task: You'll stage real Sleep-EDF PSG recordings end to end — extract EEG/EOG/EMG features, classify sleep stages with leave-one-subject-out validation, and read Cohen's kappa against the human inter-rater ceiling (≈ 0.76).

notebooks.title: Real-data track — ECG rhythm/AF (CinC-2017)
notebooks.question: Can R–R irregularity and signal-quality features separate Normal/AF/Other/Noisy ECG?
concepts: PhysioNet/CinC-2017 single-lead ECG end-to-end (open)
Band-pass, QRS detection, R–R/HRV, signal-quality index
Split by record; GroupKFold; macro-F1 / per-class recall
notebooks.task: You'll run the PhysioNet CinC-2017 single-lead ECG pipeline — Pan–Tompkins QRS detection, R-R/HRV features, and a signal-quality index — to classify normal, AF, other, and noisy rhythms with a record-level split.

notebooks.title: Real-data track — CTG / fetal (CTU-UHB)
notebooks.question: Can FHR + contractions flag a pathological delivery — and why is this honestly hard?
concepts: CTU-UHB intrapartum CTG end-to-end (ODC-BY)
Dropout removal + interpolation, baseline/variability, decel detection
Label from umbilical pH; split by recording
notebooks.task: You'll clean real CTU-UHB fetal heart-rate recordings (dropout removal, baseline, variability), build features toward a pH-based outcome label, and confront a deliberately hard, clinically realistic problem where the positive class is barely detected.

notebooks.title: Real-data track — EMG gesture (Ninapro, 2 modes)
notebooks.question: Why does a gesture classifier at 0.78 within-subject collapse to 0.19 on a new subject?
concepts: Ninapro DB1 surface-EMG end-to-end (CC BY-NC-ND)
Two eval modes: within-subject vs new-subject, side by side
Wrong-then-right: a leaky random split inflates the score
notebooks.task: You'll classify real Ninapro surface-EMG gestures two ways — within-subject and new-subject — side by side, then watch a randomly-split baseline lie to you about how well it actually generalizes.

notebooks.title: Real-data track — BCI motor imagery (EEGMMIDB, 2 modes)
notebooks.question: Why does a naive band-power baseline barely beat chance, and what would CSP add?
concepts: EEGMMIDB 64-ch motor imagery end-to-end (ODC-BY)
mu/beta ERD at C3/C4; two eval modes; chance = 0.50
An honest near-chance baseline (the advanced track's point)
notebooks.task: You'll decode real EEGMMIDB motor-imagery EEG from mu/beta power at C3/C4, see an honest near-chance baseline, and find out why the fix is a leakage-safe CSP spatial filter, not more features.
